record.original_question: Are the numbers pi, zeta(3), zeta(5), zeta(7), ... algebraically independent over Q?

evidence.quote: Conjecture 3.17. The numbers π, ζ(3), ζ(5), . . . , ζ(2n + 1), . . . are algebraically independent over Q.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
For a real number $s>1$, let $\zeta(s)=\sum_{n=1}^\infty n^{-s}$ denote the Riemann zeta function. Recall that elements $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_k\in\mathbb{C}$ are said to be algebraically independent over $\mathbb{Q}$ if there is no nonzero polynomial $P\in\mathbb{Q}[x_1,\dots,x_k]$ with $P(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_k)=0$. An infinite sequence is called algebraically independent over $\mathbb{Q}$ if every finite subfamily is.

Determine whether the numbers
$$\pi,\ \zeta(3),\ \zeta(5),\ \zeta(7),\ \ldots,\ \zeta(2n+1),\ \ldots$$
are algebraically independent over $\mathbb{Q}$.
artifact.status_search_result: This is a well-known open conjecture. It is not even known whether any single odd zeta value $\zeta(2n+1)$ with $n\ge 2$ is irrational; only $\zeta(3)$ is known to be irrational (Apéry, 1978), and Ball–Rivoal showed infinitely many odd zeta values are irrational, with results of Zudilin and Fischler giving partial quantitative refinements. Algebraic independence of $\pi$ together with all odd zeta values remains entirely open.

status_evidence.title: Irrationality of values of the Riemann zeta function
status_evidence.snippet: Rivoal's and Zudilin's results show infinitely many odd zeta values are irrational, but algebraic independence is unknown.
status_evidence.claim: Even the irrationality of most odd zeta values is open, let alone algebraic independence.

status_evidence.title: Kontsevich–Zagier, Periods
status_evidence.snippet: Conjecturally, π and the odd zeta values ζ(3),ζ(5),... are algebraically independent over Q.
status_evidence.claim: The algebraic independence of π and odd zeta values is stated as a conjecture.
